fixes.explanation: True, baker! Jacob says he sent the message “…so that I may find favor in your sight.” (Genesis 32:5) Look at the message itself. He calls Esau “my master” and himself “your servant,” and then lists his oxen, donkeys, flocks, menservants and maidservants. I think that's a man walking up to a door with a full tray and a nervous smile.

Armies sounds right with four hundred men coming, friend, and I'd have said it too. But the text says Jacob divides his people, flocks, herds and camels into two camps. (Genesis 32:7) He isn't forming a fighting force. He says if Esau attacks one camp, the other can escape (Genesis 32:8). That's a man hoping to save somebody, not win a battle.

That's the instruction, baker! Jacob entrusts the animals to his servants in separate herds and says, “Go on ahead of me, and keep some distance between the herds.” (Genesis 32:16) Picture it. Herd after herd, each one a little way behind the last, like a row of cookie sheets coming out one at a time instead of one big crowded tray. Esau meets a gift, then another gift, then another.

Right, baker! Jacob tells the lead servant what to say if Esau asks: “They belong to your servant Jacob. They are a gift, sent to my lord Esau.” (Genesis 32:18) Then he adds, “And behold, Jacob is behind us.” So the servant doesn't just answer the question, he also tells Esau who's coming up the road. I think that's a message you'd rehearse a few times before you say it out loud.
